idiom_name: discriminated union with an empty/unknown variant + assertNever; typed no-op object literal
implementation_notes: TypeScript models the special case as a variant of the value type: a discriminated union whose unknown/empty member carries no payload, narrowed by control-flow analysis so consumers see a total function, with an assertNever call (a function taking never) in the default clause turning a forgotten case into a compile error. Where the type is a collaborator interface rather than data, a frozen no-op object literal typed as that interface is the special case and costs nothing at runtime once the types are erased. Prefer the union when callers must handle the degenerate case; prefer the object when call sites should stay branch-free, and use `??` for one-line defaults - never `||`, which would also replace legitimate 0, '' and false.
pitfalls: Structural typing: any object of the right shape satisfies the interface, so a mistyped no-op still compiles; keep the special case in one module and freeze it.
Destructuring the discriminant before the switch (const { kind } = c) breaks narrowing, so the compiler can no longer prove the union is exhausted.
`||` and truthiness treat 0 and '' as absent: use `??` for defaults so legitimate values survive.
A misspelt discriminant is only caught by assertNever or a typed switch helper, not by the runtime, which silently falls through to the default branch.
